section.name: The four vowels
section.outcome: You know all four vowel marks by name, and every letter you meet afterwards gives you five syllables instead of one.

section.name: Reading real text
section.outcome: You can read a line rather than a syllable: you know what separates one syllable from the next, what ends a sentence, that nothing separates words — and you know the six letters that are not among the thirty when you meet them in a mantra.

section.name: The final test
section.outcome: You can read anything the thirty letters spell, and you can read whole words off a page you have never seen.

section.name: The thirty letters
section.outcome: You can name every one of the thirty letters and say where each one sits.

section.name: The five prefixes
section.outcome: You can read a syllable that opens with a letter nobody says — and hear what that silent letter does to the one after it.

section.name: The ten suffixes
section.outcome: You can read a syllable that ends in a consonant — all ten of them — and hear the four that bend the vowel in front of them.

section.name: The second suffixes
section.outcome: You can read a syllable with two endings, and you know the second one changes nothing.

section.name: The three superscripts
section.outcome: You can read a letter with another letter sitting on top of it, and hear which of the two things that does.

section.name: The four subscripts
section.outcome: You can read a letter with another letter tucked underneath it — and you know which of the four change the sound and which does not.

section.name: Reading any syllable
section.outcome: You can take a syllable you have never seen, find its root, and read it.

section.name: Numbers
section.outcome: You can read the ten Tibetan digits, and therefore a price.

vocabulary.en_definition: A little, a small amount. A beginner uses it constantly, most often to explain how much of the language they have.
Afternoon. Useful for arranging when to meet, which is most of what these four words do at this stage.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhito*. ཕྱ is *ch*, not "ph" followed by "y".

vocabulary.en_definition: Once more. It is the word this district turns on: come again, meet again, walk it again.
vocabulary.thl_note: *yang kyar*. The བ prefix and the ས are both silent — not "b-skyar".

vocabulary.en_definition: Someone's age. Asking it is ordinary politeness here rather than an intrusion, and it comes up early in almost any first conversation.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lo*.

vocabulary.en_definition: The thirty letters of the Tibetan writing system, learnt as a chanted series rather than read off a list. This is the doorway to the Read track and to everything written in Tibetan.
vocabulary.thl_note: *kakha khaa nga*. Four separate letters, not a word — the first four of the thirty, said as a set the way English says "ABC".
vocabulary.cultural_note: The Tibetan alphabet is learnt as a chant rather than read off a list, four letters to a line, and the chant's opening syllables name the whole series. Its order is not arbitrary: it groups letters by where in the mouth they are made, which is also the order a dictionary uses. There are thirty consonants and four vowel signs, devised in the seventh century on an Indian model rather than growing out of Chinese writing. Written Tibetan has stayed close enough to its early form that the spelling records a pronunciation from a thousand years ago rather than today's, which is why spelling is the hard part and reading aloud is a skill of its own.

vocabulary.en_definition: Also, too. The small word that adds you or a second thing to what has just been said, as in me too, or that one as well. You will hear it constantly before you need it.
Always, continually. Stronger than every day, and used of things that do not stop.
Fossilised tree resin, golden to red, used in jewelry.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Amber is worn with turquoise, coral and dzi in the same strings, and like them it is wearable property rather than only ornament — it moved with a family. Old pieces are prized and handed down, and much of what is sold as amber today is resin or plastic. It is fossilised tree resin, warm gold to deep red, and light in the hand for its size, which is why people test it by warmth and weight rather than by looking.

vocabulary.en_definition: The knotted cord worn at the neck or the wrist, and the small wrapped packet that sometimes hangs with it. It is given rather than bought, and that is the part of the word worth remembering.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sungdü*. The final ད of མདུད turns the vowel to *ü*; the མ is a silent prefix.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The knotted cord is given rather than bought, by a teacher or at a temple, and people wear one until it falls apart on its own. It is not sold, and offering money for one gets the transaction wrong; whatever is given in return goes to the place rather than for the object. When one does wear through it is not dropped in a bin: the usual course is to tie it up high, on a tree or a fence, or to burn it. The small metal box some people wear on a cord alongside it is a different object with its own name, and it holds something written rather than being jewelry.

vocabulary.en_definition: The striped apron worn over the front of a chuba, woven in narrow bands of bright color. Traditionally it marks that the woman wearing it is married.
vocabulary.thl_note: *pangden*, literally "lap-rug".
vocabulary.cultural_note: The striped apron is worn over the front of a chuba, and its traditional job is to say that the woman wearing it is married. That is still how it is read in a village, though in towns and at festivals younger women wear one without the older meaning being intended. It is woven as narrow strips and joined into panels so the stripes run vertically and the joins are part of the design, and the widths, the color order and the fineness of the weave vary by region and by how good a piece it is.

vocabulary.en_definition: Shooting at a target with a bow, as a festival contest. Held on the same ground as the racing and watched just as closely.
vocabulary.thl_note: *da gyak*. མདའ is one syllable *da* — the མ is a silent prefix and the final འ is silent.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Archery here is a festival sport rather than a hunting skill, contested between villages and between tents. Onlookers sing at the archers to put them off, and being sung at is an accepted part of the event rather than bad manners. In some places the arrows carry a pierced wooden head that whistles in flight, and the sound is half the pleasure of it. Hits are called aloud by the crowd rather than written down.

vocabulary.en_definition: Myrobalan: the small ribbed fruit held in the Medicine Buddha's right hand, and the plant that appears more often than any other in the Tibetan pharmacopoeia. It is also how you recognize the figure at a glance.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Myrobalan appears more often than any other plant in the Tibetan pharmacopoeia, and it is the fruit the Medicine Buddha holds in his right hand. That is how you recognize the figure at a glance, and it means the text and the wall of the clinic tell the same story. The tree does not grow on the plateau at all — it is a lowland one, from the warm valleys south of the Himalaya, so the fruit has always arrived by trade. Tibetan pharmacy works with three related fruits and keeps them apart by name, which is why looking up "myrobalan" in a dictionary returns three different words rather than one. The Four Tantras, the root text of the tradition, open by describing a city of medicine ringed with groves of it; what it is used for is the physician's business.

vocabulary.en_definition: The street that runs clockwise around the Jokhang, pilgrim route and market in the same space. The stalls of District 5 are on it, and the walk of District 9 follows it.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The Barkhor is the street that runs clockwise around the Jokhang, pilgrim route and market in the same space. Pilgrims making the circuit, families out for the evening and several hundred stalls all move in the same crowd at the same pace, and nobody finds the combination strange. It is a ring of roughly eight hundred metres and the direction is fixed by custom, so going the other way means pushing against everyone at once. Old Lhasa is laid out as three rings around the temple — a corridor inside it, this one around it, and a much longer circuit around the whole old town — and this is the middle of the three.

vocabulary.en_definition: The grain the plateau runs on — a hardy, quick-ripening barley that grows at altitudes where wheat will not. Roasted and ground it becomes tsampa; fermented it becomes chang.
vocabulary.thl_note: *ne*. The ས is silent and closes the vowel.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Barley is the grain the plateau runs on: roasted and ground it becomes tsampa, fermented it becomes chang, and it fed Tibet for most of its history. A valley floor of it going gold at the end of summer is the classic Tibetan landscape after the mountains themselves. Highland barley ripens fast and tolerates cold and thin air at altitudes where wheat will not grow. It is roasted before grinding, which is unusual, and that is what gives tsampa its keeping qualities and its smell: roasted flour travels for weeks and can be eaten with nothing but tea.

vocabulary.en_definition: A hand bell whose handle is shaped like the top half of a dorje, held in the left hand while the dorje is held in the right. It is one half of a pair, and it is rarely seen or spoken about on its own.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thriipu*. དྲ is a single voiced *dr*.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The bell is one half of a pair and is rarely seen alone: it is held in the left hand while the dorje is held in the right. In the meaning attached to them the bell stands for wisdom and the dorje for method, and the two are separated and brought back together at points in a ritual. Its handle is itself half a dorje, so the pair is one design cut in two, and inside the hollow there is a cast face and a ring of syllables nobody looking from outside will ever see. These are personal implements rather than fittings of a building — a monk keeps his own rather than drawing one from a store — and set down on a shrine they lie side by side.

vocabulary.en_definition: A birthday. Worth having as a word, and worth knowing that traditionally it was not an occasion at all: the year turned for everybody at once, so nobody had a private date to mark.
vocabulary.thl_note: *kyekar*. "Birth-star" — the star, not the day.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Traditionally a birthday was not an occasion: everyone gained a year together at Losar, and a child was counted as one year old at birth. The birth year mattered, though — each year in the sixty-year cycle carries an animal and an element, and that pairing is what people give when asked their age. An individual birthday therefore had little to mark, and many older Tibetans do not know the day they were born. Parties for children are now ordinary in the towns and across the diaspora, borrowed and comfortably kept.

vocabulary.en_definition: The nomads' tent: yak hair woven into cloth and pitched as a low black square with a slit along the ridge for smoke.
vocabulary.thl_note: *dra*. སྦྲ is a single voiced *br* — the ས is a silent prefix, so it is not "s-bra".
vocabulary.cultural_note: The black tent is the nomad household itself: a low square of woven yak hair with a slit along the ridge for the smoke to leave by. Inside, the hearth is central, and the working side and the guest side are settled by custom. Yak hair swells when it is wet, so the weave tightens in rain and keeps the water out while still letting the smoke through. It is guyed out to pegs some way off, which is what gives it its flattened shape, and it is woven by the family in strips and repaired strip by strip rather than replaced.

vocabulary.en_definition: Boots. The traditional kind are felt and leather with a turned-up toe, and are still worn for cold and for festivals.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lham*. The bare word; ལྷམ་གོག with གོག is the everyday "shoes".
vocabulary.cultural_note: Traditional Tibetan boots are made to be worn over layers in deep cold, and they now come out for festivals and dances as much as for the weather. They are felt and leather, soft-soled, with a turned-up toe and a tall shaft tied below the knee. The turned-up toe keeps the boot out of the snow and off rough ground, and a soft sole is easier to walk long distances in than a stiff one. Color and pattern on the shaft vary by region, so a pair says where its wearer is from in the same way an apron does.

vocabulary.en_definition: A boy. Children are the people most likely to talk to a foreigner first, so these words arrive early.
Butter, and specifically the butter of the plateau rather than a dairy shelf: churned from the milk of the dri, the female yak. It goes into tea, into tsampa, and into lamps.
vocabulary.thl_note: *mar*. One syllable.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Butter is one of the foundations of both the Tibetan kitchen and the Tibetan altar: it goes into the tea, into the tsampa, and into the lamps. It comes from the milk of the dri, the female yak, never from the yak, which is male — which is why "yak butter" is a small English error. A household buys it in quantity and keeps it as a staple, and in a market it is sold as solid blocks wrapped in cloth or hide rather than in packets. In pastoral households it was as much a good to store and to trade as one to eat.

vocabulary.en_definition: A small bowl of clarified butter with a wick standing in it, lit and set in rows in front of an image. A temple will have hundreds, and the smell of them is the smell of the building.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhöme*. The མ is a silent prefix and the ད colours the vowel to ö — not "m-chod".
vocabulary.cultural_note: A butter lamp is offered by paying for the butter and adding it to the row, often with a particular person in mind, living or dead. A temple will have hundreds standing in front of the images, and the smell of them is the smell of the building. The bowls are brass or silver, filled with clarified butter — yak butter traditionally, vegetable oil increasingly — and kept alight by attendants who top them up through the day. New lamps are lit from lamps already burning rather than struck fresh, and the heat and smoke are why the paintings in an old chapel are so dark: centuries of butter.

vocabulary.en_definition: Tea churned with butter and salt. It is savoury rather than sweet, and when someone says tea without saying which, this is often what arrives.
vocabulary.thl_note: *phööcha*. The ད of བོད is silent and colours the vowel to ö — the same ད the learner already met in བོད, `Tibet`.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Butter tea is the drink a Tibetan household runs on, and when someone says tea without saying which, this is usually what arrives. It is offered to anyone who comes through the door and your cup is refilled the moment you set it down, so leaving it full is how you say you have had enough. It is churned rather than stirred — tea, butter and salt worked in a tall wooden cylinder until they stop being three things — and at this altitude the fat and the salt are the point of it.

vocabulary.en_definition: The Tibetan calendar: a lunisolar system that counts months by the moon and keeps them in step with the sun by adding a month when the drift requires it.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lo tho*.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The Tibetan calendar counts months by the moon and keeps them in step with the sun by adding a month when the drift requires it. Households consult the yearly almanac for the timing of things, from a wedding to a journey. Days are numbered against the moon, so a date is sometimes doubled and sometimes skipped to keep the count aligned, which is why a Tibetan date moves against the Western year. It is computed rather than merely printed, and the Men-Tsee-Khang is where that work is done and where the almanac comes from. What it says on any particular day is a reading made by an astrologer; this describes the system and casts nothing.

vocabulary.en_definition: The Tibetan sitting carpet — a narrow woollen rug laid on a bench or a low platform rather than on the floor. It is what a guest is seated on.
vocabulary.thl_note: *saden*. Minimal pair with ཁ་གདན `cushion` — one syllable apart, and the difference is floor versus seat.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The Tibetan carpet is furniture rather than floor covering: a narrow woollen rug laid on a bench or a low platform, and it is what a guest is seated on. Where a guest is put, and on how good a carpet, is part of how a household says what it thinks of them. It is knotted in wool from the plateau's own sheep, whose long springy fleece is what gives the pile its resilience, and the standard size is made to seat one person. The patterns are mostly geometric or floral, with the snow lion and the dragon among the recognisable figures, and a household keeps its best ones for the shrine room.

vocabulary.en_definition: Barley beer, brewed at home rather than bought. You meet it here as a thing to recognize; this district does not teach you to order it.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhang*.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Chang is home-brewed barley beer, and it belongs to occasions rather than to evenings: weddings, harvest, New Year, and the arrival of guests. Pouring it is part of the hospitality — in many households it is offered with a set rhythm of sips and refills, and songs are sung while it goes round. It is made by fermenting cooked barley in a covered pot for a few days and comes out cloudy, mild and slightly sour rather than strong.

vocabulary.en_definition: Change: the money that comes back. Small stalls often have very little of it, so establishing this before you hand over a large note saves you a walk to find somebody who can break it.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sima*, literally "fragments" — small money, coins.

vocabulary.en_definition: Hard dried cheese made from the dri's milk, cut into small pieces and dried until it keeps for months.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Dried cheese comes from the dri's milk, and it is what makes one summer's milk last through a winter, because it keeps without cooling. It is eaten by holding a piece in the mouth until it softens, which takes a while; biting it is how visitors chip a tooth. It is dried to the hardness of a pebble and often threaded on a string. Softer fresh versions exist and go into festival dishes and sweet rice.

vocabulary.en_definition: A child, of either sex. The word you use when age matters and sex does not.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thruku*. ཕྲ is a single sound *thra*, not "ph" followed by "r".

vocabulary.en_definition: A monument of stacked geometric shapes — square base, dome, spire — built beside roads, at passes and in monastery grounds. Some hold relics or the remains of a teacher.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhöten*. This is a §8.4 anchor — known-forms.json wins over anything generated. The ར of རྟེན is a silent prefix.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A chorten is a monument people go round rather than through, keeping it on their right, and many were put up by a family or a village as an act of merit. They stand beside roads, at passes and in monastery grounds, and some hold relics or the remains of a teacher. The shape is the same everywhere, from waist-high roadside ones to the great whitewashed ones at monasteries, and its tiers are read as a set of elements stacked in order. Where one straddles a road the passage cut through it does the same job, and they are repainted rather than left to weather, which is why even old ones look new.

vocabulary.en_definition: The wraparound robe worn across the plateau: long, sleeved, and belted at the waist. It is the single most recognisable Tibetan garment.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhupa*. Two syllables; the English spelling "chuba" is a b that is not there.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The chuba is the single most recognisable Tibetan garment: a long sleeved robe wrapped across the body and tied with a sash. Because it is cut long and hitched up over the belt, the fold above the waist becomes a deep pocket that carries almost anything — a bowl, a bag of tsampa, a small child. In strong sun one sleeve is slipped off and left hanging, which is why so many photographs show one bare arm. What it is made of says where the wearer is and what the day is: sheepskin for a herder in winter, plain cloth for work, heavy silk brocade for a wedding or a festival.

vocabulary.en_definition: The tall wooden cylinder butter tea is made in, worked with a long plunger. It is the reason butter tea is churned rather than stirred.
vocabulary.thl_note: *dongmo*.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The churn is what makes butter tea butter tea: tea, butter and salt go in hot and are pumped with a plunger until they combine. In a village or a nomad camp the sound of it is a morning sound, repeated dozens of times a day. It is a narrow barrel, often banded with brass, with a plunger running its full height; in town it has largely given way to an electric blender, which is one of the few modernisations nobody argues about.

vocabulary.en_definition: The evening dance: people take hands in a ring, sing, and repeat a few steps for as long as the singing lasts. Nobody performs it and nobody watches from the edge for long.
vocabulary.thl_note: *gorshee*. སྒ is a voiced *g*; the ས is a silent prefix. Final ས of གཞས is silent.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Gorshey is the evening dance: people take hands in a ring, sing, and repeat a few steps for as long as the singing lasts. Nobody performs it and nobody watches from the edge for long — the steps are plain and repeat, so somebody arriving picks them up off the person beside them inside a verse or two. Men and women often make separate arcs of the same ring and sing in turn, one group answering the other, and the tempo climbs as the song goes on until the stamping is the loudest thing in the field. It belongs to evenings rather than to a stage: after the games, around a fire, at a wedding, at the end of a picnic. It has travelled further than almost anything else here — Tibetan communities in Toronto, Zurich and Bengaluru hold circle-dance evenings that run on the same handful of songs.

vocabulary.en_definition: A white conch shell, one of the Eight Auspicious Symbols; also a ritual instrument.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The conch's sound stands for the Buddha's teaching carrying outward in every direction, reaching whoever is in earshot. It is not only a symbol — a conch is really sounded in monasteries, to call people together. It is a white shell, blown like a horn, and one of the Eight Auspicious Symbols. A shell that spirals to the right rather than the left is rare, and those are the ones kept and decorated.

vocabulary.en_definition: Red coral, worn as beads in necklaces and in headdresses. It stands beside turquoise as the second stone of Tibetan jewelry, and the deeper and more even the red, the more it is valued.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhuuru*.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Red coral is worn as wealth rather than as decoration: a strand of good beads could represent a serious part of what a family owned. In Amdo and Kham a woman's headdress may carry dozens of large beads, assembled over many years rather than bought at once. It is a sea material worn thousands of kilometres from any sea, and it reached the plateau entirely by trade — from the Mediterranean, later from the Pacific, along the routes the tea came in on. Most of what is offered cheaply to visitors is dyed bamboo or resin, and the good pieces tend not to reach a stall at all.

vocabulary.en_definition: A country. The answer to where you are from is usually a country, so this word arrives with that question.

The black-necked crane: tall, gray-bodied, with a black head and neck and a red crown. It breeds on the high wetlands in summer and goes down to lower valleys for the winter, and it is the bird this app is named after.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thrungthrung*. ཁྲ is a single aspirated *tr*, not "kh" followed by "r". This is the app's own name.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The black-necked crane is the only crane that spends its whole life at altitude, and the bird Tibetan poetry reaches for when it speaks of leaving and returning. It nests above 4,000 metres where almost nothing else large will breed, and drops to the valleys in winter to feed in the barley stubble. The best-known four lines in Tibetan verse, attributed to the Sixth Dalai Lama, ask a crane for the loan of its wings and promise a return — the same round trip the bird makes every year. The timing is famously regular: in the Bhutanese valley where a few hundred winter, people know roughly which week the birds will arrive and which week they will go.

vocabulary.en_definition: A small two-sided hand drum used in ritual.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A small two-headed drum, held in one hand and turned rather than struck — two beaters on cords swing round and hit the heads. It is played in particular practices, usually paired with a bell in the other hand. Its shape is unmistakable: two shallow bowls joined at the narrow point, like an hourglass. It is not the big monastery drum, which is a different instrument and a different word.

vocabulary.en_definition: The day after tomorrow, in a single word rather than four. English has to build the idea out of parts each time; Tibetan keeps one word for it, and another for the matching day going backwards.
vocabulary.thl_note: *nhangnyin*. The ག is a silent prefix.

vocabulary.en_definition: The day before yesterday, again one word. Between them, the two give you five consecutive days you can name outright, with no counting in the middle.
A distance stated as the time it takes to walk it. The ordinary answer to how far away something is.
vocabulary.thl_note: *nyinlam*.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A day's walk is the ordinary answer to how far away something is, and it is a more honest unit than it sounds. A figure in kilometres says nothing about a pass at five thousand metres, a river to be crossed or snow on the far side, and a day's walk absorbs all of that. It assumes an ordinary loaded walker keeping a steady pace from light until dark, which is a shared enough picture that two people who know the ground will agree on the number. Ask in kilometres and you may well be answered in days regardless, and the days will be the more useful of the two.

vocabulary.en_definition: The formal argument monks train in, held out in a courtyard in the afternoon: one man standing and questioning, one seated and answering, with a hand-clap on each point. It is loud and physical and it is not a quarrel, which is the thing visitors most often get wrong.
vocabulary.thl_note: *tsöpa*. རྩ is a single *ts* and the ད colours the vowel to ö.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Monastic debate is loud and physical and it is not a quarrel, which is the thing visitors most often get wrong. It is the core of the study curriculum in the large teaching monasteries rather than an activity alongside it, and a monk's progress through the texts is measured by how he does in it. The standing challenger puts a question and claps once as it lands; the seated defender answers inside the terms already agreed, and the stamp, the raised arm and the clap belong to the form and carry no anger at all. The material is the fine detail of texts both sides have memorised, which is where the speed comes from, and sessions run daily for two or three hours with visitors watching from the edge of the courtyard.

vocabulary.en_definition: The eight-spoked wheel of the teaching, one of the Eight Auspicious Symbols.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The dharma wheel is the oldest way of representing the Buddha's teaching: teaching is called turning the wheel, and its eight spokes are the eight parts of the path he set out. If you learn to recognize one thing on a Tibetan roofline, this is the one. On monastery roofs it usually sits between two deer, which recalls the deer park where he taught the first time.

vocabulary.en_definition: A short metal sceptre with a ribbed sphere at the middle and prongs curving out at both ends, held in the right hand while the bell is in the left. The name is also the everyday Tibetan word for a diamond and for a thunderbolt.
vocabulary.thl_note: *dodje*. Both the ར of རྡོ and the ར of རྗེ are silent prefixes — *dorje*, not "r-do r-je".
vocabulary.cultural_note: The dorje stands for something that cannot be broken or altered, and in the pair it carries method to the bell's wisdom. The word means diamond and thunderbolt as well, which is why it is one of the commonest personal names in Tibetan — named for the quality, not the object. The shape is deliberately the same at both ends, and that is the point of it; five prongs at each end curving in onto a central one is the usual count, though nine-pronged versions exist. Cast in bronze and often small enough to close a hand around, it is carried rather than displayed, and two of them crossed form a separate design again, used as a base beneath other things.

vocabulary.en_definition: A long-necked plucked lute with six strings in three pairs, often finished with a carved horse or dragon head. The standard instrument for accompanying song and dance.
vocabulary.thl_note: *dranhyen*. སྒྲ is a voiced *dra* — the ས is a silent prefix and the whole cluster is one sound. སྙ is a palatal *ny*.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The dranyen is the instrument a Tibetan song is carried on, and it turns up wherever people are singing: festivals, picnics, homes, restaurants. The player almost always sings while playing rather than accompanying somebody else, and a capable one can hold a tent's attention for a whole evening. It is a long-necked lute with six strings in three pairs, the body carved from a single block of wood and the soundboard stretched skin, often finished with a carved horse or dragon head. Two related traditions of song and dance, nangma and toeshey, are built around it, and were played in Lhasa teahouses long before they reached a stage.

vocabulary.en_definition: The female yak, and a separate word rather than a modified one. She gives the milk that becomes the butter, the cheese and the yoghurt of the camp.
vocabulary.thl_note: *dri*. འབྲ is a single voiced *dr*; the འ is a silent prefix.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The dri is the female yak, and Tibetan keeps the two apart where English does not: a yak is male, and there is no such thing as yak milk. Nearly everything handed to a guest in a nomad camp comes from her — the butter in the tea, the dried cheese on the string, the bowl of yoghurt. She is milked early and again in the evening, and the calves are kept near the tent so that she comes back to it. Keeping dri and yak apart is one of the clearest cases of a language having exactly the words its life requires.

vocabulary.en_definition: Meat air-dried into hard dark strips and eaten as it is, without cooking. It hangs in kitchens and shops all winter.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sha kam*. Do not read it as the ཤ་སྐམ་པོ the spoken source uses of a person — that means thin, not dried.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Dried meat is eaten as it is, without cooking — torn into pieces and taken with tsampa and tea, most often through the winter. It began as nomad food and stayed everywhere, so a city shop counter and a black tent will both have some hanging. Nothing is done to it except hanging it up: the air here is cold enough and dry enough to do the preserving on its own, and it keeps for months without electricity.

vocabulary.en_definition: Dried dung, patted into cakes and stacked to dry. Above the treeline it is the fuel that boils the tea and cooks the food.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chiwa*. ལྕ is a single *ch*, not "l" followed by "c". Homograph warning: ལྕི་བ is also "heavy", which is the only sense any dictionary in the cache knows.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Above the treeline the fuel is what the herd already produces: dried dung is what boils the tea and cooks the food. This is a sensible use of the material at hand rather than a sign of poverty, and reading it as one misreads the place badly. It is gathered, shaped by hand, dried in the sun against a wall, and stacked in blocks that double as windbreaks. Burnt dry it is nearly odourless and gives a hot, clean flame.

vocabulary.en_definition: A dzi bead: a dark agate cylinder patterned with pale bands and circles, strung between coral and turquoise. It is the most prized object in the market and the most imitated.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sii*. One syllable; the ག is a silent prefix.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A dzi bead is the most prized object in the market and the most imitated — a patterned agate cylinder worn as a protective amulet. Traditionally the beads are spoken of as found rather than made, turned up in a field or inherited, which is a large part of why they are regarded as they are. The patterning was produced by a treatment nobody has convincingly reconstructed, and the pale circles are counted as eyes: how many a bead has is what settles what it is worth. A family that owns a good one will generally not sell it whatever is offered, and effectively everything sold as one in the Barkhor today is a modern imitation.

vocabulary.en_definition: A continuous, intertwined knot with no beginning and no end, one of the Eight Auspicious Symbols.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The endless knot stands for interdependence: that nothing in the world stands on its own, and that cause and effect run through everything without a loose end. You will see it on carpets, on doorways, on the corners of thangkas and printed on the paper a gift is wrapped in. It is a single line woven through itself, with no start and no finish anywhere in it. It is the one of the eight that has escaped furthest into ordinary decoration, which is why most people know the shape long before they know the name.

vocabulary.en_definition: Evening. The end of the working day and the busiest hour in a teahouse.
vocabulary.thl_note: *gongto*. The ད is a silent prefix.

vocabulary.en_definition: Every day, daily. Said of a habit rather than of a plan.
Excuse me, used to get someone's attention before you ask them anything. It is the opening move of every question you will ask in the district of Asking the Way.
A public celebration with a fixed place in the year — days of tents, food, music and games rather than a single evening.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thüüchhen*. The ས of དུས is silent and colours the vowel to ü; ཆེན is *chen*, not *chhen po* — the card is the bare compound.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A Tibetan festival is days of tents, food, music and games rather than a single evening, and it is the year's main social gathering as much as an observance. The larger ones fill a field outside town for several days: families pitch a tent, cook, visit each other and stay put. Some began as religious observances and some as agricultural markers, and Losar, the new year, is the biggest of them. They are set by the lunar calendar rather than by fixed dates, so they move against the Western year.

vocabulary.en_definition: A few days ago. Vaguer than yesterday and the day before, which is the point of it.
Food in general, as a category rather than a dish. It is the word inside the question you ask on walking into a small restaurant.
vocabulary.thl_note: *khalak*. The ཁ is aspirated and the ག closes the second syllable — not "kha-lag-pa".

vocabulary.en_definition: A foreigner, an outsider. This is the word a visitor hears applied to themselves several times a day.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhigye wa*. ཕྱ is *ch*, not "ph" followed by "y".
vocabulary.cultural_note: It is a flat description rather than an insult, closer to "not from here" than to anything colder, and it is said openly across a square or a market stall rather than behind a hand. Children use it most, usually as an invitation to be looked at. Learners of Tibetan descent hear it too, sometimes from people who assume it and sometimes from people who are checking, and that lands differently than it does on a tourist.

vocabulary.en_definition: A friend. It stretches a good deal further than the English word and covers the person you have been drinking tea with for an hour.
vocabulary.thl_note: *throokpo*. གྲ is a voiced *dr*, not "g" followed by "r".

vocabulary.en_definition: Full, said of a cup rather than of a person. It pairs with empty, and it is the state your cup will be in every time you look down at it.
vocabulary.thl_note: *khaang*. One syllable, and it leans on the noun in front of it — ཇ་གང is heard as one word, *jagang*.

vocabulary.en_definition: The full moon, and with it the fifteenth of a Tibetan month, since the months are counted from the moon. It is a date as much as a sight, and a good deal of the year hangs off it.
vocabulary.thl_note: *tshepa chongha*. བཅོ་ལྔ is *chonga*, the irregular fifteen — not "cho-lnga".
vocabulary.cultural_note: The full moon falls on the fifteenth of a Tibetan month, and the fifteenth and the thirtieth are the month's observance days. A kora is noticeably busier on them, more households go without meat, and monastic communities hold their twice-monthly assembly. The fifteenth of the fourth month, Saga Dawa, is the largest of them, and the Lhasa circuit is crowded from well before dawn. A Tibetan month begins at the new moon, which keeps the number and the sky in agreement most of the time, though days are occasionally doubled or dropped to keep the count in step with the sun, so the calendar's fifteenth and the astronomer's full moon can sit a day apart.

vocabulary.en_definition: The future, time still to come. It is the word for later in general, not for a particular later.
Generally, on the whole. It softens a claim you do not want to make absolutely.
A girl. The pair to boy, and equally likely to be the person addressing you.
A pair of golden fish, one of the Eight Auspicious Symbols.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The golden fish stand for living without fear and without being held in place: a fish moves through water in any direction it likes. They are always a pair, usually facing each other, and they also stand for fertility and plenty, from the sheer number of fish in a river. It is one of the older symbols in the set and predates Buddhism in India.

vocabulary.en: goodbye (said to the one who is leaving)
vocabulary.en_definition: The goodbye said to the person who is leaving. Tibetan has two, and this is the one you use when you are the one staying behind.
vocabulary.thl_note: ཕེབས is the honorific of "to go"; the b is not pronounced — *phe*, not *phebs*.

vocabulary.en: goodbye (said to the one who is staying)
vocabulary.en_definition: The goodbye said to the person who is staying. This is the one you use when you are the one walking out of the door.
vocabulary.thl_note: བཞུགས is *shu* — the b and the final s are both silent. An English reader will want "b-zhugs".

vocabulary.en_definition: A double-reed wind instrument played in monastic ceremony.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The gyaling carries the melody in monastic music, where the long horns carry the drone. If you have heard a recording of Tibetan monastic music, this is the reedy, insistent sound in the middle of it. It is a double-reed instrument with a decorated wooden body and a flared metal bell — much closer to an oboe than a flute, despite the look of it. It is played in pairs, with drums, cymbals and long horns around it.

vocabulary.en_definition: A hat. At this altitude the sun is fierce enough that a wide brim is practical rather than decorative, and hats are worn all year.
vocabulary.thl_note: *shaamo*. The ྭ under ཞ is not pronounced as a separate sound.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A hat is worn all year here, and it is one of the things a region can be recognised by: the shape, the brim and the trim differ from place to place. At this altitude the sun is fierce enough that a wide brim is practical rather than decorative. The fur-trimmed winter hat with fold-down flaps and the wide felt or straw hat of the grasslands are both ordinary, and a good one is brought out for a festival.

vocabulary.en_definition: The heart as the organ in the chest. The Kora teaches a separate word for the heart as the seat of feeling and thought, and the two are not interchangeable.
One word covering what English splits into 'heart' and 'mind': where you think and where you feel, treated as the same place.
vocabulary.cultural_note: English divides thinking from feeling and puts them in different organs. Tibetan does not make that split in ordinary speech — one word does both jobs, and being happy, being upset, being kind, remembering, deciding and intending all happen there. It is why a lot of Tibetan expressions about character read oddly in translation: 'good-hearted', for a decent person, is not a metaphor about the emotions, it is a plain description of where the goodness sits. Once you have noticed it, a good deal of the vocabulary in this district lines up behind it.

vocabulary.en_definition: A lake regarded as sacred, with a walking route round its shore. The big ones take several days to get round.
vocabulary.thl_note: *nhetsho*. The ག of གནས and the མ of མཚོ are both silent prefixes.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A sacred lake is walked round the way a mountain is, and sacred in practice includes keeping the water clean — nobody washes or swims in them. Three in particular draw walkers: Yamdrok, Namtso and Manasarovar, each with a shoreline route and a scatter of small monasteries and cave hermitages along it. Getting round one on foot takes days, camping as you go, and the weather can close the route at either end of the season. They are high, cold and an intense turquoise, linked to particular protector figures, and one of them carries a long association with divination.

vocabulary.en_definition: A mountain regarded as sacred, walked around rather than climbed. Several are destinations in their own right and draw walkers from across the plateau.
vocabulary.thl_note: *nheri*. The ག of གནས is a silent prefix.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A sacred mountain is walked around rather than climbed — the route, not the summit, is the point, and the best-known peaks have deliberately never been climbed. Particular mountains are understood as the homes of particular deities, which is why a specific peak matters rather than mountains in general. A full round of Mount Kailash in the far west is roughly fifty kilometres, crosses a pass over five and a half thousand metres, and takes most walkers three days. Buddhist and Bön walkers take the same route in opposite directions and pass each other all day.

vocabulary.en_definition: The place your family is from, which is not necessarily anywhere you have lived. This, not your current address, is usually what a Tibetan means when they ask where you are from.
vocabulary.thl_note: *phayü*. The final ལ colours the vowel to ü rather than sounding as an l.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The word is built on the word for father, and it names an ancestral place rather than a residence, which is why two Tibetans meeting will establish it within a minute of each other. Knowing it locates a person: it says which region they belong to, roughly how they will sound, and often who the two of you both know. In the diaspora it is answered with complete confidence by people who have never set foot there, since it is inherited rather than visited, and exile communities are frequently organized into associations along exactly these lines. It also carries a good deal of the feeling in Tibetan song, which is full of home places described from a long way off.

vocabulary.en_definition: The long telescopic horn, several metres of it, played in pairs from a roof or a courtyard. The note is very low and carries across a valley.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The long horn is what people mean when they say they can hear a monastery from the far side of a valley. Its job is to mark the shape of a ceremony and to be heard at a distance rather than to carry a tune: a low drone with rises, sounding a very small number of notes. It extends in sections to three or four metres and is played resting on the ground or on a stand, usually two together, with players using circular breathing to keep the note unbroken. Together with the shorter horns, cymbals and drums it makes the sound that carries furthest out of a monastery.

vocabulary.en_definition: A race ridden over open ground, and the center of a summer festival. The riders are often boys, and the horses are the working horses of the district.
vocabulary.thl_note: *ta gyuk*. རྟ is a single sound *ta* — the ར is a silent prefix, so it is not "r-ta". རྒྱ is a voiced *gy*.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The horse race is the center of a summer festival, and winning carries standing for the horse's owner and their family well past the day itself. Families camp for the duration and the racing shares the ground with archery, wrestling, trading and a good deal of visiting. Alongside the flat races there are displays of picking objects off the ground at a gallop and of shooting from the saddle. The preparation starts months ahead, and the largest gatherings, on the eastern grasslands, run to thousands of tents.

vocabulary.en_definition: A house — the building rather than the household. Traditional town houses are stone or mud brick, flat-roofed, and built around a courtyard.
vocabulary.thl_note: *nang*.

vocabulary.wylie: khyed rang sku gzugs bde po yin pas
vocabulary.thl: khyé rang ku zuk dé po yin pé

vocabulary.en_definition: Ground aromatic wood and herbs, burnt as a stick or loose on a fire so that the smoke rises. In monasteries and on hillsides it is burnt at the start of the day.
vocabulary.thl_note: *pö*. The ས prefix and the final ས are both silent and the vowel rounds to ö — the written "spos" and the said *pö* have almost nothing in common.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Incense is offered rather than used as a room scent: the smoke going up is the point of it. It is burnt at the start of the day at monasteries and on hillsides, and the smell reaches you well before you can see where it is coming from. Tibetan incense is usually a plain dough of ground juniper and herbs, extruded and dried without a bamboo core, so the whole stick burns away. Juniper branches are also burnt loose in a masonry hearth, which is what produces the thick white smoke at a monastery gate, and recipes differ by region and by monastery — people are particular about which they buy.

vocabulary.en_definition: A vessel for burning incense.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A vessel for burning incense, from a plain clay pot in a house to worked metal in a temple. Incense is offered daily, and it is also used to clear and settle a room before anything else happens in it. In many homes the first act of the morning is lighting it. Outdoors the same thing is done at a much larger scale, burning juniper in a kiln-shaped hearth at a monastery gate or on a pass.

vocabulary.en_definition: The temple at the center of the old town, and the point everything else in Lhasa is described in relation to. Ask the way to it from anywhere in the old streets and somebody can point.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The Jokhang is the temple at the center of the old town and the point everything else in Lhasa is described in relation to. It holds the statue pilgrims cross the plateau to stand in front of, and its courtyard flagstones are worn into hollows by people prostrating in the same spots for centuries. Founded in the seventh century, it is far older than anything else standing in the city, and it faces west rather than towards the mountains behind it. The smoke on the approach is juniper burning in the two kilns outside the doors, and the street running clockwise around it is the Barkhor, so temple, market and pilgrim circuit are the same few hundred metres of ground.

vocabulary.en_definition: The thick white smoke of juniper branches burnt in the morning — at a monastery gate, on a hilltop, at the top of a pass. The smell of it reaches you well before you can see where it is coming from, and it is one of the things people remember longest about being here.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sang*. The བ is a silent prefix — *sang*, not "b-sang".
vocabulary.cultural_note: Juniper smoke is the offering, not the fire: the point is that it rises and spreads. It is burnt at first light at monasteries and by households on their own roofs, so a Tibetan town at dawn has smoke going up from a dozen places at once. Fresh branches are burnt in a low masonry hearth, often with tsampa, butter or barley thrown on top, and travelers burn it again on reaching the top of a pass. Juniper grows slowly at these altitudes and good branches are carried a long way to reach the place they are burnt.

vocabulary.en_definition: A long scarf of thin white silk or cotton, offered with both hands. It is given on arrival, on departure, at weddings, at the start of a journey, and at almost every occasion in between.
vocabulary.thl_note: *khatak*. The བ prefix and the final ས are silent. This is one of section 8.4's anchored forms — if the generated THL disagrees with known-forms.json, the table wins.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A khata is a ceremonial scarf offered to show respect, welcome, gratitude or good wishes, and it marks almost any occasion that matters. It is given to teachers and elders, to a couple marrying, to a guest arriving and to someone leaving, and draped over statues and photographs. It is offered with both hands and a slight bow, and the person receiving it very often puts it straight back around the giver's neck, so it travels in both directions. White is the standard color, associated with sincerity and good intention; a finer one in five colors is the more formal offering.

vocabulary.en_definition: A walk clockwise around something held sacred — a temple, a monastery, a mountain, a whole city. The word covers both the walk and the path it follows.
vocabulary.thl_note: *korra*. The ས is a silent prefix. This is a section 8.4 anchor — known-forms.json wins over anything generated.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A kora is a walk made clockwise around something held sacred — a temple, a monastery, a mountain, a whole city — done as an act of devotion. That does not stop it also being the daily exercise and the place where people meet and talk; the devotional and the social are not separate here. Some koras take twenty minutes; the circuit of Mount Kailash takes several days, and pilgrims who measure their length along the ground rather than walking take weeks. The Bön tradition, which runs alongside Buddhism in Tibet and is older, goes the other way round, anticlockwise, and going the wrong way at a Buddhist site is the most visible mistake a visitor makes and the easiest to put right.

vocabulary.en_definition: Cold mung-bean noodle, cut into slippery strips and dressed with chilli, vinegar and garlic. It is eaten standing at a stall rather than sitting in a restaurant.
vocabulary.thl_note: *laphing*. A Chinese loan (涼粉 liángfěn), so the syllables carry no Tibetan meaning.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Laping is the thing eaten between things — a cold mung-bean noodle under chilli oil, bought standing at a stall in the middle of the afternoon. The stalls cluster around the Barkhor and are run overwhelmingly by women, and the chilli on it is far hotter than anything else in this kitchen. The noodle is a set jelly rather than a dried strand: mung-bean starch cooked to a paste, left overnight to firm up in a tray, then cut into ribbons or shaved into curls. It came in from Chinese cooking and has been absorbed so thoroughly that Lhasa now argues about whose version is correct.

vocabulary.en_definition: Last night, yesterday evening. The one arrangement here that is not simply the two obvious words joined, so it is worth hearing on its own.
Later, at some point after this. It is deliberately vague, which is exactly what makes it useful: it lets you leave a conversation without fixing a time to anything.
vocabulary.thl_note: *djela*. རྗ is a single *j*.

vocabulary.en_definition: Tibetan opera: a sung and danced drama performed outdoors, with masks, a narrator and a chorus. A performance runs for hours and sometimes across days.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lhamo*. ལྷ is a single voiceless *lh*, one sound, not "l" plus "h".
vocabulary.cultural_note: Tibetan opera is played in the round on flat ground, with the audience sitting on all sides and coming and going as they please. The stories come from history and from well-known tales and everyone already knows how they end, so the audience eats, talks and plays cards throughout. A narrator sets each scene in verse and a chorus answers the singers, and masks and color do the work a costume would do elsewhere, telling you who a character is before a word is sung. Troupes travel to summer festivals, and a performance runs for hours and sometimes across days.

vocabulary.en_definition: Lhasa: the city this walk moves through, and the source of the variety of Tibetan taught here.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Lhasa is the city Tibetans mean when they say the city — the seat of the Jokhang temple and the destination of pilgrims from every part of the plateau. Its old town is arranged in rings around that temple, and the street circling it is pilgrim route and main market at once. It sits at about three and a half thousand metres on the Kyichu river, high enough that most arrivals spend their first day short of breath, and its speech is what standard spoken Tibetan means.

vocabulary.en_definition: Losar, the Tibetan New Year: the largest festival of the year, on the first day of the first Tibetan month, which puts it in February or March.
vocabulary.thl_note: *losar*. The ག of གསར is a silent prefix.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Losar is the largest festival of the year, and its shape is fixed: the first day at home, the second visiting, the third going out. The days before are for cleaning the house out completely and for a noodle soup on the eve, with small objects hidden in the dumplings for everyone's amusement but the finder's. New prayer flags go up over the roofs and the greeting is exchanged with everybody. Because the date comes out of the lunisolar calendar it moves in the Western year, and it does not always fall with the Chinese New Year.

vocabulary.en_definition: The lotus flower, one of the Eight Auspicious Symbols.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The lotus stands for purity that comes through the mud rather than by avoiding it — a flower that grows up out of mud and opens clean, without a mark on it. Almost every buddha and bodhisattva in Tibetan painting is seated or standing on one. When you next look at a thangka, look at what the figure is standing on: it is nearly always this.

vocabulary.en_definition: A string of beads used to keep count of recitations, worn on the wrist or held in the hand. You will see them everywhere, often moving while their owner is doing something else entirely.
vocabulary.thl_note: *threngwa*. ཕྲ is a single aspirated *thr* — not "ph" then "r".
vocabulary.cultural_note: A mala is what a recitation is counted on, and you will see them everywhere, often moving while their owner is doing something else entirely. One bead is passed for each repetition, worked through with the thumb, and at the head the string is turned back rather than crossed. The standard string has 108 beads and a larger head bead, with small counter strings hanging off some malas for keeping track of completed rounds. Bone, wood, seed and stone are all ordinary materials, and a mala moving in somebody's hand during a conversation is not inattention.

vocabulary.en_definition: A man. One of the first words you need to describe someone you have just met to somebody else.
vocabulary.thl_note: *kyepa*. The ས prefix and the final ས are both silent.

vocabulary.en_definition: A flat stone carved with a written mantra and left beside a path. They gather into long walls and heaps at passes, river crossings and the edges of villages.
vocabulary.thl_note: *mani do*. ཎ is the retroflex n of the Sanskrit mantra, pronounced as an ordinary *n*.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A mani stone is a flat stone carved with a mantra and left beside a path, added and never taken away. They gather into walls that grow at the rate of the traffic past them, so some are hundreds of metres long and centuries deep, with the oldest stones buried inside. Carving them is a trade as well as an act of devotion: carvers work at the roadside and are paid to add a stone on someone else's behalf. Walkers pass with the wall on their right, which is why a mani wall down the middle of a path has a lane on either side of it.

vocabulary.en_definition: A short fixed formula, said over and over, usually under the breath and counted on a mala. On the kora it is the sound underneath everything else: hundreds of people murmuring, none of them loudly.
vocabulary.thl_note: *nghak*. སྔ is a single sound *ng*; there is no "s" before it.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A mantra is a short fixed formula said over and over, and on the kora it is the sound underneath everything else. It is done while doing other things — walking, waiting, sitting on a bus — which is why it can take a visitor several days to notice how much of it is going on. The one heard most is the six-syllable mantra associated with Avalokiteshvara, the figure of compassion, and it is the same text carved into mani stones and rolled up inside prayer wheels. It is counted rather than simply repeated: a mala of a hundred and eight beads is worked round, and people keep running totals over years. The syllables are Sanskrit rather than Tibetan and are kept in an approximated pronunciation rather than translated, because the sound itself is held to be the working part.

vocabulary.en_definition: Marriage, as a thing rather than as something you do. It is here mainly because whether you are married is one of the first questions a stranger will ask you, put without any of the awkwardness an English speaker expects.
A face worn by a performer, made of painted cloth, papier-mâché or carved wood. It announces which character you are looking at from the far side of a field.
vocabulary.thl_note: *bak*. འ is a silent prefix. One syllable.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A mask announces which character you are looking at from the far side of a field, and color is the main code. A blue mask, a white mask and a half-red mask each signal a particular kind of character to an audience that grew up watching. They fall into two families: the flat cloth ones of opera, and the heavy carved and painted ones worn in monastic masked dance. The dance masks belong to the monastery that holds them and are stored rather than displayed, brought out for dances that fall on set days in the calendar — town events, watched by everyone.

vocabulary.en_definition: Maybe, perhaps. The softener for when yes and no are both too strong — an invitation you have not decided about, a plan that may not happen. It leaves the question open without committing you to anything.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chik chheena* — གཅིག is *chik*, not "g-chig".

vocabulary.en_definition: Sangye Menla, the Medicine Buddha: the blue figure at the center of a Tibetan medical room, a sprig of myrobalan in one hand and a bowl in the other. Where a clinic elsewhere might hang a diagram, this is what is on the wall.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Sangye Menla, the Medicine Buddha, is the blue figure at the center of a Tibetan medical room, where a clinic elsewhere might hang a diagram. He holds a sprig of myrobalan in one hand and a bowl in the other, and the lapis blue is the same in every painting, which makes him easy to identify. The tradition holds that the Four Tantras were taught by him in a city of medicine surrounded by the plants they describe, so the textbook and the image on the wall are one story told twice. Students of Tibetan medicine have traditionally begun their training with him rather than with anatomy, and paintings often show eight such figures together rather than a single one. Describing that is as far as this card goes; the practice belongs to the people who keep it.

vocabulary.en_definition: Midday, noon. It is a stretch of the day rather than a point on a clock, and it fills the gap between morning and afternoon in the sequence you are learning here.
Midnight. Less immediately useful than the other time words and here to complete them, though it earns its place in District 13, where long-distance buses leave at hours like this one.
A dumpling, steamed or fried, filled with meat or vegetables. If one dish stands in for the whole cuisine, it is this one.
vocabulary.thl_note: *mokmok*, two identical syllables. The ག of the first syllable is not heard as a separate consonant.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The momo is the dish that stands in for the whole cuisine: a dumpling, steamed or fried, filled with minced meat and onion or with greens and cheese. They belong to New Year, holidays and visitors rather than to a quiet Tuesday, because they are made in batches by several people at a table talking. The dough is rolled and pleated by hand and how neat the pleats are is noticed, and the same dumpling under a similar name turns up all across the Himalaya and well beyond it.

vocabulary.en_definition: Money. The general word, for what changes hands rather than for any particular note or coin.
vocabulary.thl_note: *nghü*. The ད is silent. It is also the word for the metal silver — see `silver`.

vocabulary.en_definition: Morning. It is a piece of time you can talk about, not a greeting: there is no separate good morning to learn.
vocabulary.thl_note: *shookpa*.

vocabulary.en_definition: A person's name. Asking for someone else's name and offering your own are handled by separate fixed phrases in this district, so you are never asked to pick between them yourself.
vocabulary.thl_note: *ming*.

vocabulary.en_definition: A Nepali person. Worth having early: much of the diaspora passed through Nepal, and in Lhasa the word is heard about traders.
Night. The stretch after everything has closed, rather than a time you arrange to meet in.
vocabulary.thl_note: *tshenmo*. The མ is a silent prefix. Same syllable as མཚན, `name` (H) — a real collision worth telling the learner about once.

vocabulary.en_definition: The polite negative answer, for correcting a wrong guess about you without any sharpness. You will need it the first time someone assumes you are from somewhere you are not.
Now, at this moment. It is one of the most used words in any language and easy to skip past in a wordlist, and it turns up in nearly every arrangement you will hear made.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thaata*. ལྟ is a plain *ta*, and the whole word is heard as two light syllables — not "da l-ta".

vocabulary.en_definition: The row of seven small bowls of water set out in front of a household shrine. They are filled in the morning and emptied in the evening, and the row is one of the first things you notice in a shrine room.
vocabulary.thl_note: *yönchhap*. ཆབ is the honorific word for water, which is why it is also inside ཆབ་གསང `toilet`.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The seven bowls offer a guest what a house would put in front of one: water to drink, water to wash with, flowers, incense, light, scented water and food. Plain water stands in for all of them because it is the one thing a household can give without limit, so nothing about the offering is grudging. They are filled with clean water each morning and set in a straight line with a small even gap — touching is avoided and so is spacing them widely. In the evening the water is poured out and the bowls are dried and stacked upside down, so the row is set up and taken down again every day of the year. Doing it is part of the ordinary running of a house rather than a specialist job, and it usually falls to whoever is up first.

vocabulary.en_definition: All right, fine, agreed. The general-purpose word for accepting what has been said or offered.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lakso* — the s of ལགས closes the syllable rather than starting a new one.

vocabulary.en_definition: A ceremonial parasol, one of the Eight Auspicious Symbols.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The parasol stands for protection — shelter from suffering and from harm, the way a parasol shelters from sun. Real ones are carried over a lama in procession, so the symbol and the object are the same thing. Anywhere in Asia a parasol held over someone marked their standing, because it meant a person was employed to carry it, and in Buddhism that becomes protection. It is a parasol on a long handle, fringed and often silk.

vocabulary.en_definition: A high saddle between peaks, where a road crosses a range. On the plateau a pass, a la, is a named place with a marked summit rather than merely the top of a hill.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lakha*. ཁ here is "top, mouth of" — the top of the la, not a separate word to learn.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Crossing a pass is treated as a small arrival: the vehicle stops, everyone gets out into the wind, and the shout goes up. The summit carries a cairn of stones and a mass of prayer flags, and travelers add a stone as they cross. A pass is a named place with a marked summit rather than merely the top of a hill, and it is also where the weather turns and where the altitude is felt hardest.

vocabulary.en_definition: A person, in the general sense. Useful for counting people in a room or saying who a thing belongs to.
A summer outing to a spot by water, with a tent, cooking gear and enough food for days. Nearer a small camp than a lunch.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lingka*. གླ is a single sound *l*, not "g" followed by "l" — the ག is a silent prefix. This is the *linka* of ནོར་བུ་གླིང་ག Norbulingka.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Around Lhasa the summer picnic is an institution rather than an outing: nearer a small camp than a lunch, and it can last a week. Visitors who wander past tend to be absorbed into whichever tent they are nearest, and declining the food takes considerably more effort than accepting it. Families put up a canvas tent in a park or a grove by the river and bring stoves, thermoses, cards and dice; the tents are white with blue appliqué patterns and go up in rows. The season runs through the warm months, when the barley is in the ground and there is a gap in the work.

vocabulary.en_definition: The small brown-gray pills of Tibetan medicine, ground from plant and mineral ingredients and rolled by hand. They are the usual form a Tibetan prescription arrives in.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The herbal pill is the usual form a Tibetan prescription arrives in — small, brown-gray, and rolled by hand. The formulas are recorded in the medical texts and made up at the Men-Tsee-Khang, and larger pills are wrapped in coloured cloth and crushed or dissolved rather than swallowed whole. A pill is a compound rather than a single ingredient: many components, ground, blended to a written formula, rolled damp into a bead and dried. What any particular pill is for is a matter between a physician and a patient, and describing the form is as far as this goes.

vocabulary.en_definition: The word that softens a request. You always meet it inside a whole phrase in this track, so you never have to decide where to put it.
vocabulary.thl_note: *roknhang*. The dictionary's English→Tibetan hits for "please" (མགུ་བ, "to gratify") are the wrong sense entirely.

vocabulary.en_definition: The palace on the hill above the city, visible from most of it. It is the landmark visitors ask for most often and the easiest to steer by, because you can usually just look up and find it.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The Potala is the palace on the hill above Lhasa, visible from most of the city, and for many Tibetans it is the single image that stands for Tibet itself. From the seventeenth century it was the seat of the Tibetan government and the winter residence of the Dalai Lamas; it is a museum now. It climbs thirteen storeys on the site of a much older fort — the white outer sections held the offices and living quarters, the red block at the center the chapels and the tombs of eight Dalai Lamas. There is no steel in it and very little foundation: the walls are stone and rammed earth, metres thick at the base and tapering as they rise, which is what has kept it up.

vocabulary.en_definition: A pecha — a book of loose oblong leaves printed on both sides, stacked between two wooden boards and wrapped in cloth. It is not bound and does not open like a Western book.
vocabulary.thl_note: *pechha* — the English word for the object is borrowed from this one, so the card is teaching a word the learner may already own.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A pecha is not bound and does not open like a Western book: loose oblong leaves stacked between two wooden boards and wrapped in cloth. A reader unties the wrap, sets the stack down and moves each leaf aside as they finish it, so the book is worked through as a pile rather than turned. Pecha are kept high rather than on the floor, and are not stepped over or sat on. The format came from Indian palm-leaf manuscripts and kept the long narrow shape long after the material changed to paper, and the boards range from plain planks to carved and painted ones.

vocabulary.en_definition: A printed cloth flag, strung in long lines from rooftops, bridges and mountain passes, in a fixed sequence of five colors.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thaarchok*. ལྕ is a single *ch* — not "l" then "c".
vocabulary.cultural_note: Prayer flags are strung in long lines from rooftops, bridges and passes so that the wind moving over them carries the printing outward. They are meant to fade — cloth bleached blank by sun and wind has done its work, and new lines are strung over the old rather than the old taken down. The five colors run in a set order, blue, white, red, green and yellow, standing for sky, air, fire, water and earth, and each flag is block-printed with text and images. Passes are the densest place to see them, layered there by travelers over many years.

vocabulary.en_definition: A cylinder on a spindle with printed text rolled up inside it, turned by hand or set in rows along a wall to be turned by people passing.
vocabulary.thl_note: *mani khorlo*. The འ of འཁོར is silent — *khorlo*, not "'khor lo". ཎ is the retroflex n of the Sanskrit mantra and sounds like an ordinary n here.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A prayer wheel holds a tightly wound scroll printed with a mantra, and turning it is understood to have the same effect as saying what is inside. Rows of them run along monastery walls to be turned by anyone going past, which is what the stream of people beside them is doing. They are turned clockwise, the same direction as a kora, and sizes run from a hand wheel with a weighted chain to fixed wheels taller than a person, some of them driven by water.

vocabulary.en_definition: Before, previously, in the past. It points backwards without saying how far.

The full-length bow: down to the ground, arms stretched out in front, and up again. People do them on the spot along the kora, and some do them the whole way round, measuring the circuit with their own body.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhaktshe wa*. ཕྱ is a single sound *ch*, not "ph" + "y".
vocabulary.cultural_note: A prostration is a gesture of respect before anything else, made towards teachers and images rather than only at buildings. It goes hands together to the head, the throat and the heart, then down until the body is flat with the arms out, then up. Doing them in sets in one place is common, and the boards worn smooth outside a temple are where people do them; pilgrims prostrating along a road move forward by their own length each time, marking where their hands reached, which is how journeys of many months are made. Those covering ground wear wooden mitts and a leather apron rather than staying put. It is among the most photographed things in Tibet and among the easiest to photograph thoughtlessly, which is worth knowing before you raise a camera.

vocabulary.en_definition: Rope, usually twisted from yak hair. A camp runs on it: guy lines, tethers and loads.
A riding saddle built up at front and back on a wooden frame, and covered with rugs.
vocabulary.thl_note: *ga*, one syllable. Homograph warning: སྒ is also the word for ginger, which is what every dictionary in the cache returns for it.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A saddle is the piece of a herder's equipment most likely to be decorated, and a good one is handed down rather than replaced. It is dressed for a festival the way a rider is: worked metal at the front and back, and saddle rugs in bands of color under and over it. The frame is wooden, built high at front and back so that a rider sits into it rather than on top of it, which is what makes a long day in it possible. Motorbikes have taken over much of the daily herding, so a full set of saddle and rugs now comes out mostly for racing and for festivals.

vocabulary.en_definition: A sacred design made from coloured sand, built and then deliberately swept away.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A sand mandala is swept up when it is finished and the sand carried to a river — that is the teaching, not an afterthought. Something made this beautifully and this slowly is still let go, because everything is. It is a sacred design made from thousands of grains of coloured sand, laid down through a narrow metal funnel. Monks may work on one for days or weeks, and every line follows a set plan rather than an artist's choice.

vocabulary.en_definition: The written form of the language — the shapes themselves, as distinct from the words they spell. Tibetan has one alphabet, written in more than one hand.
vocabulary.thl_note: *yiksuuk*. གཟུགས is *suk* — the ག prefix is silent.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Tibetan script carries a standing well beyond reading: letters are carved into rock, painted on cliffs and printed on cloth where nobody expects to read closely. There is one alphabet written in two broad styles — an upright printed form and a faster cursive one — and the same thirty letters serve both. It was devised in the seventh century on an Indian model and has changed very little since, which is a large part of why spelling and speech have drifted so far apart. It is also used for several other languages of the region, and it is more regular than it looks, because the same shapes repeat.

vocabulary.en_definition: A flat round pastry stuffed with minced meat and fried. It is the thing eaten with tea, and in many teahouses it is the only food on the counter.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sha phaaklep*. Literally meat-bread: ཤ meat + བག་ལེབ bread, both of which the source teaches separately.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Shabaley is what is eaten with tea, and in many teahouses it is the only food on the counter. It is one of very few Tibetan dishes that is street food rather than something a family makes at home, cooked in front of you in a wide pan of oil and eaten standing up. A disc of dough is sealed around spiced minced beef, crimped shut at the edge and shallow-fried until the surface blisters, so it comes out somewhere between a pie and a fritter. The name travels with the food and gets written several different ways on menus in Lhasa, in Dharamsala and in Queens, none of which is wrong.

vocabulary.en_definition: Sho, the dice game played across teahouse tables. It is the second thing happening in the room after conversation, and the noise of it is the sound of the place from the street.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sho*. One syllable, and the game is ཤོ་རྒྱག་པ *sho gyakpa* — the same རྒྱག verbaliser the source uses for playing cards.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Sho is the dice game played across teahouse tables, and after conversation it is the second thing happening in the room. Players call out as they throw, in set phrases and often in rhyme, and the calling is half the game — a good player is entertaining as well as fortunate. The dice are thrown from a wooden cup slammed down onto a leather pad, with shells or coins moved around the rim as counters, and the slam is what makes a teahouse audible from the street. It is largely a men's game and largely an afternoon one, small amounts of money change hands, and somebody standing and watching is welcome as long as they are not in the way of the throw.

vocabulary.en_definition: The room in a house kept for the family shrine. It is usually the best room in the building, and it is not a spare room used for other things.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhökhang*. མཆོད is *chö* — the མ is silent.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Most Tibetan households keep a room, or at minimum a wall, for the shrine, and it is very rarely absent altogether. It generally gets the best light and the best carpets in the house, and formal guests are received there. The altar holds images, photographs of teachers, butter lamps, and seven small bowls of water set out in the morning and emptied at night. The daily upkeep falls to whoever is at home rather than to a specialist, and in a small flat the whole thing shrinks to a shelf.

vocabulary.en_definition: A woven wool sling, used to throw a stone past the herd so that the animals turn without being touched.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The sling is how a herder steers: a stone landed beyond an animal, on the side it should move away from, turns the herd without anything being touched. Often the crack of it in the air is enough on its own. Slings are woven from wool in patterned bands and worn round the waist or over the shoulder, so they serve as a belt when they are not in use.

vocabulary.en_definition: Slowly. It is a word in its own right, and it also sits inside both goodbyes, which is why learning it stops them being two opaque noises.
vocabulary.thl_note: *khaaler*. The ག is unvoiced at the start of a word.

vocabulary.en_definition: The snow leopard: the pale gray, heavy-tailed cat of the high crags. Herders know it as the animal that takes livestock, and almost nobody, herders included, ever sees one.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sa*, one syllable — the ' is the འ suffix and is not a glottal stop for the learner to produce.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Herders know the snow leopard as the animal that takes livestock, and almost nobody, herders included, ever sees one. It lives mostly on blue sheep, hunting by getting above them on a slope and dropping, and takes goats when wild prey is thin, which is where the trouble with herders begins. The tail is nearly as long as the animal, used for balance on rock and wrapped around itself when it lies down, and it cannot roar — the noises it makes are closer to a house cat's than to a lion's. Some monasteries have long forbidden hunting on the mountains behind them, and surveys have found a meaningful share of the plateau's cats living on exactly that ground.

vocabulary.en_definition: The snow lion: white, with a turquoise mane, and an emblem rather than an animal anybody has met. It is on flags and carvings and holding up the thrones inside temples.
vocabulary.thl_note: *khaang sengke*. The ས of གངས is silent.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The snow lion is an emblem rather than an animal anybody has met: white, with a turquoise mane, holding up the thrones inside temples and standing on flags and carvings. It appears in pairs far more often than singly — two hold up a throne, two flank a doorway, two face each other on old Tibetan coins.
