The mane and the eyebrows are turquoise, which is the quickest way to tell it from any other carved beast on a beam. It is one of the four figures at the corners of a windhorse print, alongside the tiger, the garuda and the dragon, and there is a dance for it as well, performed by two people inside a single costume.

vocabulary.en_definition: A permanently snow-capped peak. It is its own category in Tibetan rather than a mountain that happens to have snow on it.
vocabulary.thl_note: *khaangri*. The ས of གངས is silent and nasalises into the ར.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A snow mountain is treated as the residence of a local deity and the protector of the district below, so a peak is a neighbor addressed by name rather than scenery. Villages orient themselves by their peak, and it is often the first thing named when someone tells you where they are from. It is its own category in Tibetan rather than a mountain that happens to have snow on it, and several are, by local preference, not climbed at all.

vocabulary.en_definition: Sorry. An apology for something you did or bumped into, rather than a way of getting attention.
vocabulary.thl_note: *gongtak*. The དག prefix is silent; not "d-gongs d-ag".

vocabulary.en_definition: The stove in the main room — cooking, heating and the place everybody sits around, all at once. It is where the family is, so it is where a guest is taken.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thap*. Also the ཐབ inside ཐབ་ཚང, kitchen.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The stove is where the family is, so it is where a guest is taken: cooking, heating and the place everybody sits around, all at once. Its position sets the seating order — the places nearest the warmth go to elders and to guests, and being moved towards it is being honoured. The traditional stove burns dung or wood and stands at or near the center of the main room, which is the one reliably warm spot in a house with no other heating, and tea is kept hot on it all day. Bottled gas and electric rings have arrived in the towns, but the arrangement of a room around its center has not changed much.

vocabulary.en_definition: Black tea boiled with milk and sugar, served by the glass. It is the other tea, and in a Lhasa teahouse it is what most people are drinking.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Sweet tea is what most people in a Lhasa teahouse are actually drinking: black tea boiled with milk and sugar, served by the glass. The teahouses run on a simple arrangement — you sit, put coins on the table, and someone comes past with a thermos, filling your glass and taking payment from the pile. It came over the Himalaya from India and Nepal rather than out of the older Tibetan kitchen, and has been so thoroughly adopted that an afternoon can be spent on very little, which is what these places are for.

vocabulary.en_definition: A table. In a teahouse it is low, long and shared, and it belongs to the room rather than to you. The same word does duty in the restaurant and the guesthouse later on.
vocabulary.thl_note: *choktse*.

vocabulary.en_definition: The all-purpose greeting, safe with anyone at any hour of the day. It is the first thing you will say off the bus and the last thing you will stop needing.
vocabulary.cultural_note: It is a good wish rather than a report on the time of day, which is why one form covers morning, evening and every stranger in between. The same words carry the New Year, so it always keeps a faint edge of celebration. Said with a small bow of the head it becomes formal; said quickly across a market stall it is ordinary courtesy.

vocabulary.en_definition: The bowl a person drinks tea from, often wooden and personal to them.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The tea bowl is personal: people carried their own inside the fold of the chuba and used it wherever they went. Your host refilling it before it is empty is not impatience, it is the ordinary courtesy of the room. It is a shallow wooden bowl, and the thing Tibetan butter tea is actually drunk from. A good one is turned from a burl and can be extremely valuable; a plain one is an everyday object.

vocabulary.en_definition: Noodle soup made with dough torn into rough squares by hand rather than cut into strands. It is heavier and more homely than thukpa, and it is what gets cooked when the weather turns.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thenthuk*, from འཐེན་པ "to pull" — the noodles are pulled by hand, which is the whole difference from thukpa.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Tenthuk is what gets cooked when the weather turns: noodle soup made with dough torn into rough squares by hand rather than cut into strands. It belongs to the household more than to the restaurant, which is why a bowl of it in somebody's kitchen is reliably better than a bowl of it on a menu. The dough is rolled flat then pulled and pinched straight into the boiling broth, so no two pieces are the same shape and the soup thickens as it goes. It sits inside the thukpa family rather than beside it: the name is what distinguishes the torn kind from the rest.

vocabulary.en_definition: A painting on cloth, mounted in a brocade surround with a dowel at the bottom so that it can be rolled up and carried. They hang in temples and in the shrine room of a house.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A thangka is a painting on cloth that rolls — mounted in brocade with a dowel at the bottom, so it travels, which mattered in a country of long journeys. They hang in temples and in the shrine room of a house, behind a silk curtain that is lifted to show the painting rather than left open. It is painted on primed cotton to a measured grid: the proportions of each figure are set by manuals, so the painter's freedom lies in the landscape, the color and the fineness of the line rather than in the composition. Mineral pigments, and powdered gold on the expensive ones, give them their depth.

vocabulary.en_definition: Thank you. The words are literally "great kindness", which is why it can sound warmer than the English and is worth using more often, not less.
The thermos flask that stands on the table and does the refilling. It is the single most present object in this district.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The thermos is the most present object in a Tibetan room: it holds the tea, so tea is available continuously and without ceremony. Almost every table, kitchen, shop counter and long-distance bus has one, and a guest arriving is a thermos being lifted. They are usually enamelled or painted with flowers and kept full from morning to night, and refilling a cup costs nobody anything, which is why it happens constantly.

vocabulary.en_definition: These days, lately. It frames what is true now against what used to be, and it opens a great many conversations about home.
Noodle soup: broth, noodles, some meat or vegetables, served scalding in a deep bowl. The ordinary evening meal.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Thukpa is the ordinary evening meal: noodles in broth with some meat or vegetables, served scalding in a deep bowl. It is winter food in a place with a long winter, and a bowl of it is the standard answer to somebody arriving cold and late. It is a family of dishes rather than one recipe — noodles pulled long, cut short, or torn into rough squares — and every household makes it slightly differently and is confident theirs is correct.

vocabulary.en_definition: Tibet: the plateau this whole walk is set on, most of it lying above four thousand metres.
vocabulary.thl_note: *phöö*. The ད is silent and colours the vowel; not "bod".
vocabulary.cultural_note: Tibet is the highest inhabited region on earth, a plateau ringed by the Himalaya on one side and desert on the others, where altitude decides what grows and what is eaten. So the staple is barley rather than rice, the fat butter rather than oil, and tea is drunk salted and hot all day. It is also large enough that the Tibetan of one valley is hard work for someone from another, and for many Tibetans abroad it is a place they are from and have never been.

vocabulary.en_definition: A Tibetan person. You will hear it as a question about yourself more often than you expect, especially if you look as though you might be.
vocabulary.thl_note: *phööpa*. The ད is silent and colours the vowel to ö.

vocabulary.en_definition: To arrive, to reach somewhere. You meet it inside "When did you arrive?", one of the first questions anyone will put to you, and that sentence is learned whole. The card is here so the verb is recognisable when it comes round again on the pilgrimage road.
vocabulary.thl_note: *leppa*. The ས prefix is silent — not "s-leb".

vocabulary.en_definition: To ask, in the sense of putting a question to someone. This card is here to be recognised rather than said: the place you actually use the verb is the whole sentence "Can I ask you something?", which you learn in one piece. Seeing the verb alone is only so that you notice it again inside the sentence.

To greet. You meet it inside "Please greet your family for me", which is where it does its work, and the card exists so that the word is familiar when it turns up elsewhere. There is nothing to produce here; recognising it is the whole task.

To hear. The working form is the phrase "Sorry, I can't hear you well", which is more useful than it sounds in a courtyard with several conversations going on. The verb on its own is for recognition; it is not something to produce.

To introduce, in the sense of presenting one person to another. The sentence you actually use is "Let me introduce my friend", drilled as a single piece; this card asks only that you recognize the verb sitting inside it.
vocabulary.thl_note: *ngotrö shuuwa*. སྤྲ is a single *tr*, not "s-p-r".

vocabulary.en_definition: To talk, to speak. The phrase "Please talk slowly" is where you use it, and that phrase is learned whole. This card asks only for recognition, so that the verb stops being an unidentified sound in the middle of a sentence you already know.
vocabulary.thl_note: *ke chha shepa*, literally "to speak words".

vocabulary.en_definition: Today. The first of the three day-words, and the one that turns up in nearly every arrangement you make.
Tomorrow. It closes the district: the last phrase you learn here is see you tomorrow.
Tomorrow evening. Tibetan builds this from tomorrow and evening exactly as English does, so it is two words you already have.
Tonight, the evening of the day you are already in. It is what you need to make a plan that does not require naming a date.
An offering sculpture built from barley dough and butter, shaped by hand and set on the altar. They run from a plain cone the size of a fist to coloured constructions taller than a person.
vocabulary.thl_note: *torma*. The ག is a silent prefix.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A torma is an offering sculpture set on the altar, built from barley dough and butter, and much of it is made to be taken apart or burnt when the ritual ends. The work is temporary on purpose, and the shape, color and size are specified in writing rather than left to the maker. This is a trained job inside a monastery rather than a decorative one, and some monasteries produce butter sculpture of extraordinary fineness for particular festivals, worked with hands kept in cold water so the butter does not soften. They run from a plain cone the size of a fist to coloured constructions taller than a person, and what stands on an altar all year round is often a permanent version in painted wood or metal, standing in for the dough one.

vocabulary.en_definition: A decorated vase symbolising inexhaustible abundance, one of the Eight Auspicious Symbols.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The treasure vase stands for abundance that does not run out — long life, prosperity, and enough of what is needed. The point of it is the not running out rather than the wealth. It is round and richly decorated, usually shown with jewels spilling from the neck or a plant growing out of it. Vases of this shape are also filled and buried or placed in buildings as a blessing on the place.

vocabulary.en_definition: Roasted barley flour, the staple food of the plateau. It is mixed by hand with butter tea in a bowl into a soft dough and eaten as it is.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Tsampa is the staple of the plateau and the food most bound up with who Tibetans are — across dialects and borders people have described themselves as tsampa eaters. Roasted barley flour needs no cooking: add butter tea, work it against the side of the bowl with the fingers, and eat. That makes it food you can carry for days on a road with no kitchens, which is what it was for centuries of herding, trade and pilgrimage. A pinch of it is thrown into the air at Losar and at other moments of good wish, so it turns up in celebration as well as at breakfast.

vocabulary.en_definition: A small clay image or miniature chorten, pressed out of a mold and left where it was made. You will see them stacked in niches, in rock hollows and in the little shelters beside a path.
vocabulary.thl_note: *tsatsa*. Both syllables are the unaspirated *ts*, not *tsh*.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A tsatsa is placed rather than given, and not taken away again: a niche fills over years, the oldest at the bottom crumbling back into the clay they came from. You will see them stacked in rock hollows and in the little shelters beside a path, and weathering is not treated as damage. They are made by pressing damp clay into a carved or cast mold; one mold turns out hundreds, and making a great many at a sitting is the usual form rather than making one carefully. The clay is sometimes mixed with something else — grain, powdered plants, or the ashes of somebody who has died, which is how a family may come to have a set made after a death. Small ones now turn up on stalls aimed at visitors, which sits awkwardly with what they are for.

vocabulary.en_definition: Turquoise: the blue-green stone worn set in silver at the ears, at the throat and in the hair. With coral, it is what Tibetan jewelry is built out of.
vocabulary.thl_note: *yu*. One syllable — the ག is a silent prefix written before ཡ with no stacking.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Turquoise is worn set in silver at the ears, at the throat and in the hair, and a good piece is a family asset rather than an ornament — worn daily, inherited, and sold when money is needed. With red coral it gives the combination that reads as Tibetan at a glance anywhere in the world. Color matters more than size: the stone shifts towards green as it ages and takes up oil from skin, so a bead worn for forty years does not look like a new one, and there are people who prefer each. There is also a very great deal of dyed howlite and molded plastic sold in the Barkhor, which is exactly why asking whether a stone is real is a phrase worth having.

vocabulary.en_definition: The upright, headed script: every letter hangs from a straight horizontal stroke along the top. This is what books, signs and woodblocks are written in.
vocabulary.thl_note: *uchen*, and the THL matters here more than anywhere else in the district because this is the word the Read track says on its first screen. དབུ is *u*: the ད prefix and the བ are both silent, and it is the honorific word for 'head'. Not 'du-chen', not 'bu-chen'.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Uchen is the formal form of the script: carved into blocks and stone, painted on walls, used for anything meant to last. The line of heads across the top is what gives a page of Tibetan its ruled look, and the reason it reads as printed even when it is hand-drawn. It is the easier of the two to learn, since the shapes are regular and stay separate from each other. Because handwriting is usually not uchen, somebody who reads print comfortably can still be stopped by a note.

vocabulary.en_definition: The headless cursive script — the same alphabet written without the top stroke, faster and more joined up. This is what people write by hand.
vocabulary.thl_note: *ume*, with the accent — 'u-may', not 'u-med'. Same silent དབ as `uchen`; མེད is *mé*, the ད silent.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Umé is what people actually write by hand: take the head-stroke away and a letter can be made in a single movement. Letters, notes and accounts are written in it, and it is what you will be handed if you ask somebody to write their name down for you. It has several hands of its own, from a careful book style down to a running shorthand. Reading print comfortably does not mean you will read umé, and learners often meet it as a surprise rather than as a next step.

vocabulary.en_definition: Usually, as a rule. The honest middle between always and sometimes, and the safest of the three for a beginner.

Very. It strengthens whatever it is attached to, and it is the difference between the plain thank you and the strengthened one you already know. Learning it late means two fixed courtesies stop being two unrelated noises.
A cylindrical ceremonial banner, one of the Eight Auspicious Symbols.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The victory banner marks victory — not over an enemy, but over obstacles, over ignorance, over the things in a person that get in their own way. You can see them in metal on the roofline of almost any large temple, usually in a pair flanking the dharma wheel. It is a tall cylindrical banner of stacked, decorated tiers, flown from monastery roofs.

vocabulary.en_definition: A person's voice — the sound of them, recognised down a phone or across a room.
vocabulary.thl_note: *ke*. One syllable, and it is everywhere in the course already: བོད་སྐད Tibetan language, སྐད་ཆ conversation, སྐད་གཏོང་བ to call someone over. The learner will meet it as "language" long before they meet it as "voice".

vocabulary.en_definition: A wedding. Long, crowded and measured in days rather than hours, with a guest list running well past what an English wedding would attempt.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhangsa*. Literally "chang place" — the beer names the event.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A Tibetan wedding is measured in days rather than hours and moves between houses: the bride's family first, then the journey to the groom's, then the reception there. Khatas are the currency of it, given at every arrival and hung round necks in layers until people wear a dozen at once. Barley beer is poured continuously, and there is a set way of taking the first cup, in three sips with it topped up between each. The date is usually settled by consulting an astrologer, which can move a wedding months from where the two families first wanted it. Songs are exchanged between the bride's side and the groom's, each expected to field singers, and that part carries on long after the formal business has finished.

vocabulary.en_definition: Well, in good health. This is the ordinary answer when somebody asks how you are, and the one you will give most often.

vocabulary.roman: khyerang khii tshen la khaare re
vocabulary.wylie: khyed rang gi mtshan la ga re red
vocabulary.thl: khyé rang gi tsen la ga ré ré

vocabulary.en_definition: The wild yak, the drong. Tibetan gives it its own word rather than treating it as a yak with an adjective, and a bull is roughly twice the size of the herded animal — something herders keep well clear of.
vocabulary.thl_note: *drong*. འབྲ is a single voiced *dr*, the same cluster as འབྲི.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The wild yak has its own word in Tibetan, drong, rather than being a yak with an adjective, and the herded animal is descended from it rather than merely related. A bull can approach a tonne and stand near two metres at the shoulder, which is something herders keep well clear of. They live in the Changtang, the empty northern plains, in country too high and too dry for anyone to keep animals of their own. A wild bull will sometimes take domestic females out of a herd, and the calves that come of it are prized and hard to handle in about equal measure. In the Aru basin there is a population with pale golden coats instead of the usual brown-black, rare enough that seeing one is a story a herder tells for years.

vocabulary.en_definition: Lungta: the small printed paper squares thrown into the air at the top of a pass. Each one has a horse in the middle of it, which is where the name comes from.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lungta*. རླ is a single sound, *l* — the ར is silent; རྟ is *ta*.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Lungta are the small printed paper squares thrown into the air by the handful at the top of a pass, so the ground beyond the cairn is usually littered with them. In ordinary speech the same word does duty for a person's spirits or luck, and which sense is meant comes from what is being talked about. Each square carries a horse at its center with a jewel on its back, and a tiger, a lion, a garuda and a dragon at the four corners. They are sold in bundles at the roadside below a pass, and the same word covers the strings of cloth flags, which is why one name turns up for both the paper and the fabric.

vocabulary.en_definition: A woman. Pairs with the word for man; both come up constantly in the courtyard conversation this district models.
vocabulary.thl_note: *phüüme*. The ད of བུད is silent and turns the vowel to ü.

vocabulary.en_definition: A rectangular block of hardwood with one page of text carved into it, in mirror image and in relief. One block prints one page, and is carved on both faces.
vocabulary.thl_note: *parshing*. Literally 'print-wood'.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A woodblock holds one page carved in mirror image, and blocks last for centuries and are still inked and printed from rather than kept behind glass. A large work runs to thousands of them, shelved on end like books; the biggest houses hold tens of thousands. A block is cut from seasoned birch or another hard wood, planed flat, and carved by hand after a scribe has written the page out and pasted it face-down onto the surface. The carver works in reverse and cannot undo a slip without patching in a plug of wood, so the checking is done before the cutting rather than after.

vocabulary.en_definition: The male of the plateau's high-altitude cattle. A yak is male: the female is a dri, and Tibetan does not use one word for both.
vocabulary.thl_note: *yak*. The ག is a silent prefix attached to ཡ (Wylie g.yag) — one syllable, and the ག is never heard. Not a cluster and not "g-yak".
vocabulary.cultural_note: A yak is male — the female is a dri, and Tibetan does not use one word for both, because the two animals do different work every day of the year. A yak carries loads, pulls a plow, and gives hair for tent cloth and rope, dung for fuel, and meat and hide at the end of its life. The milk, though, comes from the dri, which makes "yak butter" and "yak cheese" quietly wrong in every language that says them.

vocabulary.en_definition: The counting word for years of a life, as in "twenty years old". It belongs to age specifically, not to years on a calendar.
The short, polite way of agreeing with what someone has just said. It is the safe answer: it commits you to nothing beyond agreement.
Yesterday. Completes the set of three, so you can place something before, on, or after the day you are standing in.
Set yoghurt from the dri's milk: thick, sharp, and eaten plain, with sugar, or stirred into tsampa.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Fresh yoghurt is the height of the summer at a camp, when the animals are giving the most milk. Set overnight in a wooden pail from the dri's milk, it arrives thick enough to stand a spoon in, and is eaten plain, with sugar, or stirred into tsampa. Lhasa has a summer yoghurt festival, at which yoghurt was traditionally offered to monks coming out of the summer retreat, and which is now known mainly for its opera performances.

phrase.roman: ka dri shiik shuu na drikkire pe
phrase.en_definition: Can I ask you something? The opener that makes a question to a stranger feel less abrupt, and the natural next step after excuse me. It also puts the verb ask in front of you inside a whole sentence, which is the only way this track ever teaches a verb.
phrase.en_literal: speech (H) — ask — a — do (humble) — if/when — all right — will/does — ?
phrase.wylie: bka' 'dri zhig zhu na 'grig gi red pas/
phrase.thl: ka dri zhik zhu na drik gi ré pé

phrase.en_definition: I don't understand. The sentence that gets you out of trouble when a conversation has run away from you.
phrase.en_literal: I — understand — not — did (I witnessed it)
phrase.usage_note: This is a survival phrase and it comes in the first stop of the district, before anything you might want to say. Knowing the escape hatch first makes the rest less frightening.

phrase.en_definition: Excuse me, used to open a conversation with a stranger.
phrase.usage_note: Say this before the question, not instead of it. Every direction you ask in District 6 starts here.

phrase.en_definition: Goodbye said to the person who is leaving, by the person staying put. If you are seeing someone off at the door, this is yours.
phrase.usage_note: Getting the two goodbyes the wrong way round is the most common beginner slip in this district, and it is charming rather than rude. The test is simple: whose feet are about to move.

phrase.en_definition: Goodbye said to the person staying, by the person leaving. If you are the one picking up your bag, this is yours.
phrase.usage_note: The two goodbyes are usually said in the same breath, one from each side, which is a good way to hear the difference.

phrase.roman: khyerang khii nang mir tsham dri shuu rok nhang
phrase.en_definition: Please greet your family for me. Said as you part from someone whose household you know, or have just heard about. It is ordinary courtesy rather than a formality, and it carries more warmth than the English sounds like it should.
phrase.wylie: khyed rang gi nang mir 'tshams 'dri zhu rogs gnang /
phrase.thl: khyé rang gi nang mir tsam dri zhu rok nang

phrase.en_definition: The greeting itself, spoken as a complete turn. It works walking into a shop, sitting down beside someone, or answering the door.
phrase.usage_note: There is no time-of-day greeting to choose between, so this one form covers the whole day. Do not go looking for a separate good morning.

phrase.en_definition: The reply to a greeting, which is the same form said back. The whole exchange is one word answered by the same word.
phrase.usage_note: This is worth practicing as a pair rather than alone. The thing to learn is that nothing changes on the way back.

phrase.en: "I want to have a conversation with you."
phrase.wylie: khyed rang dang skad cha bshad 'dod yod/
phrase.thl: khyé rang dang ké cha shé dö yö

phrase.wylie: ngas khas len byed kyi yin/
phrase.thl: ngé khé len jé kyi yin

phrase.wylie: ngas tshod dpag byed kyi yod/
phrase.thl: ngé tsö pak jé kyi yö

phrase.en_definition: Thank you, la. The little word on the end is the politeness marker you will hear attached to almost everything anyone says to you, and it is shown here fixed to a phrase because it never stands on its own. Adding it to what you already say is the cheapest way to sound courteous rather than blunt.
No, it isn't. Correcting a wrong assumption without argument.
phrase.usage_note: Drilled whole, as one fixed answer. You are never asked to build the negative yourself.

phrase.en_definition: No, thank you. The polite refusal: a third cup, a second helping, something you are being shown at a stall. A bare no lands flatly in most languages, and this is the version that does not.
phrase.en_literal: yes/(H particle) — is not (of myself) · heart (H) — lord/compassion — great

phrase.roman: khaaler ke chha sung rok nhang
phrase.en_definition: Please talk slowly. This is the standing request, for a conversation running faster than you can follow, rather than for one sentence you missed. Say it early, while you can still follow the thread.
phrase.wylie: ga ler skad cha gsung rogs gnang /
phrase.thl: ga ler ké cha sung rok nang

phrase.en_definition: Please say it again slowly. The follow-up to saying you did not understand.
phrase.usage_note: The pair works better than either half alone: say you did not understand, then ask for it again slowly. People almost always oblige, and often loudly, which is not the same thing as slowly.
phrase.wylie: yang bskyar ga ler gsung rogs gnang /
phrase.thl: yang kyar ga ler sung rok nang

phrase.en_definition: I'm sorry. An apology for something small: a bump in a crowd, a spilt cup, being late.
Thank you, as a complete turn. Use it for tea poured, directions given, change handed back.
Thank you very much, for a real favor rather than routine service.
phrase.usage_note: Keep it for the times it is earned. Used for everything it stops meaning anything.
phrase.wylie: snying thag pa nas thugs rje che/
phrase.thl: nying tak pa né tuk jé ché

phrase.en: "You are welcome here." (said to an arriver)
phrase.en_definition: You are welcome here. Said to someone who has just arrived — at a door, at a table, in a shop. In Tibetan it is a full sentence rather than a single word, which is why it sits among the phrases and is taught as one fixed thing.

phrase.wylie: ngas ga re lab dgos red/
phrase.thl: ngé ga ré lap gö ré

phrase.en_definition: Yes, that's right. Confirming what someone has just said about you or about the situation.
The reply to thanks, closer to "it was nothing" than to a formal you're welcome.
phrase.usage_note: You will hear it more than you say it at first. Recognising it is enough for now.

phrase.roman: ku khyen ngatsho khalak nghak na drikkire pe
phrase.en_definition: Excuse me, we'd like to order. The sentence that gets a table served, and one you may need twice in a busy room. It opens with the excuse me you learned in District 1, doing exactly the job it was taught for.
phrase.en_literal: body (H) — «མཁྱེན» · we — food — «མངགས» — if/when — all right — will/does — ?
phrase.wylie: sku mkhyen/_nga tsho kha lag mngags na 'grig gi red pas/
phrase.thl: ku khyen nga tso kha lak ngak na drik gi ré pé

phrase.en_definition: Do you have change? Asked when you are holding a note that is far too large for what you are buying.
phrase.usage_note: Worth asking early rather than at the end. Small stalls often genuinely do not have it, and the answer may be that you go and buy something else first.

phrase.en_definition: And you? Handing the same question straight back.
phrase.en_literal: you — also — well — is it? (of you)
phrase.usage_note: Two words that keep a conversation going when you have run out of everything else. Learn it attached to how are you rather than on its own.
phrase.wylie: khyed rang yang bde po yin pas/
phrase.thl: khyé rang yang dé po yin pé

phrase.en_definition: Are you married? An ordinary early question rather than a personal one, and it is asked of visitors constantly, often in the same breath as your age. Expecting it takes all the surprise out of it.
phrase.en_literal: you — marriage — did/struck — do you have?
phrase.wylie: khyed rang chang sa brgyab yod pas/
phrase.thl: khyé rang chang sa gyap yö pé

phrase.en_definition: Are you Tibetan? A question you will be asked as often as you ask it.
phrase.en_literal: you — a Tibetan — is it? (of you)
phrase.usage_note: Answering it is what the yes and no from District 1 are for. Both answers are fixed forms you have already met.
phrase.wylie: khyed rang bod pa yin pas/
phrase.thl: khyé rang bö pa yin pé

phrase.roman: khyerang khong ngoshe ki yö pe
phrase.wylie: khyed rang khong ngo shes kyi yod pas/
phrase.thl: khyé rang khong ngo shé kyi yö pé

phrase.roman: khye rang ku suuk de po yin pe
phrase.en_definition: How are you? Asked of someone you have just met or have not seen for a while.
phrase.en_literal: you — body (H) — form — well — is it? (of you)
phrase.usage_note: There are several versions of this at different levels of politeness. The one taught here is the safe choice with a stranger; the others are worth recognising before they are worth using.
phrase.wylie: khyed rang sku gzugs bde po yin pas/
phrase.thl: khyé rang ku zuk dé po yin pé

phrase.en_definition: How old are you? A normal, friendly question here rather than a delicate one.
phrase.en_literal: you — «དགུང» — age — how much — is (I know it of myself)
phrase.wylie: khyed rang dgung lo ga tshod yin/
phrase.thl: khyé rang gung lo ga tsö yin

phrase.en_definition: Sorry, I can't hear you well. For a noisy courtyard, a bad phone line, or someone speaking very quietly. It is a different problem from not understanding, and saying which one you have gets you a more useful answer.
phrase.en_literal: sorry — ? — good — hear/understand — not — did (I witnessed it)
phrase.wylie: dgongs dag ngas yag po go ma song /
phrase.thl: gong dak ngé yak po go ma song

phrase.en_definition: I'm a foreigner. A quick, unbothered way of accounting for yourself.
phrase.en_literal: I — a foreigner — is (I know it of myself)
phrase.usage_note: It works well as a preface to speaking badly on purpose, and it usually earns patience rather than a switch to English.

phrase.en_definition: I'm from ___. Your answer, with a place name dropped in.
phrase.en_literal: I — ___ — from — is (I know it of myself)
phrase.usage_note: The other of the two fill-in phrases. A country, a city or a region all sit in the blank equally well, and nothing else in the sentence moves.

phrase.en_definition: I'm not very well. Honest rather than dramatic, and genuinely useful in the first days at this altitude.
I'm well. The ordinary answer, and the one you will use nearly every time.
phrase.en_literal: I — well — is (I know it of myself)

phrase.en_definition: I'm ___ years old. Your answer to the age question.
phrase.en_literal: I — age — ___ — is (I know it of myself)
phrase.usage_note: You learn it now with one fixed number in it, because the numbers themselves arrive at the Market in District 5. It opens up properly once you have them.

phrase.roman: nge throokpo ngotrö shuu khii yin
phrase.en_definition: Let me introduce my friend. Said when you are the one who knows both people, which happens sooner than you would think once you are staying somewhere. It also hands a conversation to someone who did not have one.
phrase.wylie: nga'i grogs po ngo sprod zhu gi yin/
phrase.thl: ngé drok po ngo trö zhu gi yin

phrase.en_definition: My name is ___. Your half of the exchange, with your own name dropped in.
phrase.en_literal: my — name — ___ — is (I know it of myself)
phrase.usage_note: This is one of only two places in the whole track where you fill a blank yourself, and the blank takes a name and nothing else. Nothing around it changes, whatever name you put in.

phrase.roman: khyerang djel ne sempa ga chhuung
phrase.en_definition: Pleased to meet you. Said after names have been exchanged, closing the introduction.
phrase.en_literal: you — meet (H) — from — heart — like/glad — happened (to me)
phrase.wylie: khyed rang mjal nas sems pa dga' byung /
phrase.thl: khyé rang jel né sem pa ga jung

phrase.en_definition: See you later. The looser goodbye, for someone you expect to run into again the same day. It sits beside see you tomorrow, which commits you to an actual time; this one does not.
See you tomorrow. The natural way to end a first conversation that you intend to continue.
phrase.usage_note: It pairs with the two goodbyes rather than replacing them: this first, then whichever goodbye fits who is walking away.

phrase.roman: theering khong nghösu sheel djel chhuung
phrase.wylie: de ring khong dngos su zhal mjal byung /
phrase.thl: dé ring khong ngö su zhel jel jung

phrase.en_definition: What is your name? The opening question of a first conversation, once you have greeted someone.
phrase.usage_note: The person you meet in this district is called Dawa, which means moon, and why so many Tibetans are named after planets is something you will find out later on.
phrase.wylie: khyed rang gi mtshan ga re red/
phrase.thl: khyé rang gi tsen ga ré ré

phrase.en_definition: When did you arrive? The standard follow-up to where you are from, and a question you will be asked far more often than you ask it. Recognising it is worth more here than being able to produce it.
phrase.en_literal: you — when — to arrive — is (I know it of myself)
phrase.wylie: khyed rang ga dus slebs pa yin/
phrase.thl: khyé rang ga dü lep pa yin

phrase.en_definition: Where are you from? The second question of almost every first conversation, and often the first if you look like a visitor.
phrase.en_literal: you — from where — is (I know it of myself)

phrase.en_definition: 'Lha gyal lo', the shout given at the top of a pass. It is the one utterance in this district that is not part of a conversation.
phrase.usage_note: Called out as the vehicle reaches the top, by everybody in it. A visitor joining in is met with approval rather than surprise.
phrase.cultural_note: Lha gyal lo is what a Tibetan calls out on reaching the top of a pass — victory to the gods, shouted into the wind at the moment of crossing. A handful of printed paper squares goes up with it, scattered over the cairn and the flags, and travelers of every kind take part. A pass is a threshold, and a threshold is marked rather than simply passed; the flags strung across it are there for the same reason.

phrase.roman: nga yang choktse di dramla de na drikkire pe
phrase.en_definition: May I share this table? Teahouses fill up and tables are shared by default, so this is the ordinary way to sit down rather than an imposition on anyone. Ask, then sit; the answer is almost always yes.
phrase.en_literal: I — also — table — this-of — «འགྲམ» — to/at — stay — if/when — all right — will/does — ?
phrase.wylie: nga yang cog tse 'di'i 'gram la bsdad na 'grig gi red pas/
phrase.thl: nga yang chok tsé di dram la dé na drik gi ré pé

read_rule.statement: A prefix or superscript takes the breath out of a low root.
Suffixes ད ན ལ ས front the vowel before them.
ལྷ is the one stack with a superscript that you can hear. It makes a sound the thirty do not have on their own — a breathy l, high, written lhha.
The ten digits, written left to right like the words.
A tsheg separates one syllable from the next, a shad closes a clause and a nyis shad a section — and nothing separates words.
A prefix is written and never pronounced.
The reading procedure, in order: root, then what is above and below it, then the vowel, then the suffix.
Find the མིང་གཞི — the root is the letter everything else hangs off.
The thirty sit in eight rows. Rows 1-4 have four columns: unaspirated, aspirated, voiced, nasal.
Six letters are not among the thirty: five are mirror images of letters you already read, and one is a stack. Recognise them; never spell with them.
ལ takes the syllable over: ཀླ གླ བླ རླ སླ are all read lha — an l, raised. ཟླ is the exception and is read da, low.
ར pulls the root back — ཀྲ is tra, not kra — and it does it to the velars, the dentals and the lip letters alike. But ས and མ are untouched: སྲ is still sa, མྲ still ma.
ཝ is silent. It changes nothing at all — it is there to tell two spellings apart.
ཡ sits under a root, and the root's family decides what happens: the velars ཀ ཁ ག keep their sound and gain a y-glide; the lip letters པ ཕ བ མ move to the palate and end up sounding like ཅ ཆ ཇ ཉ.
Each of the ten suffixes has its own final sound, or none.
ས may follow the suffixes ག ང བ མ. It is silent and changes nothing else.
A superscript is silent, and what it does depends on the root: it takes the breath out of ག ཇ ད བ ཛ, which stay low; it lifts ང ཉ ན མ to a high tone. Never both.
Four written marks, and the absence of a mark is the inherent a.
Wylie spells what the stack hides.
